tasks.description: Write a function `is_palindrome(s)`. Use `assert` statements to test it with 'racecar' (True) and 'hello' (False).
tasks.hint:
`assert condition, 'error message'` — raises AssertionError if condition is False.
`assert is_palindrome('racecar') == True`
`assert is_palindrome('hello') == False`
Assertions are quick tests — great for simple checks.
tasks.solution:
def is_palindrome(s):
    s = s.lower()
    return s == s[::-1]

assert is_palindrome('racecar') == True
assert is_palindrome('hello') == False
assert is_palindrome('Madam') == True, 'should ignore case'
print('All assertions passed')
tasks.walkthrough:
Each `assert` checks one case. If any were false, Python would stop with an AssertionError and the final print would never run.
Seeing the message means every check passed.

tasks.description: Write a `TestPalindrome` class using `unittest.TestCase`. Add test methods for True cases, False cases, and edge cases.
tasks.walkthrough:
Three test methods group related checks: things that should be palindromes, things that shouldn't, and edge cases like empty strings.
`unittest.main` discovers every method starting with `test` and runs them, reporting a dot for each pass.

tasks.description: Run your tests using `unittest.main()`. Understand the output: dots for passing, E for errors, F for failures.
tasks.hint:
At the bottom: `if __name__ == '__main__': unittest.main()`
Dots (`.`) = test passed; `F` = assertion failed; `E` = unexpected exception.
The final line shows `OK` or the number of failures.
tasks.walkthrough:
This run deliberately includes one passing test, one failing assertion (F) and one that raises an unexpected exception (E), so you can see all three symbols.
The summary at the end lists each failure with its traceback and finishes with FAILED and the counts.

tasks.description: Use `setUp()` in your test class to create shared test data before each test method runs.
tasks.hint:
`def setUp(self):` runs before EACH test method — use it to set up state.
`self.palindromes = ['racecar', 'madam', 'level']` — shared across all tests.
This avoids repeating setup code in every test method.
tasks.walkthrough:
`setUp` builds the two word lists before each test, so each method has fresh copies to work with.
The tests loop over the lists, and the message argument names the word if a check fails.

tasks.description: Use `self.assertRaises()` to test that your function raises the right exception for bad input.
tasks.hint:
`with self.assertRaises(ValueError): my_function(bad_input)`
The test passes if the ValueError is raised; fails if it isn't.
This tests that your error handling works correctly.
tasks.walkthrough:
`is_palindrome` raises TypeError for anything that isn't a string, and these tests confirm that.
`assertRaises` as a context manager passes only if the expected exception happens inside the `with` block.

lesson.intro:
Tests are small programs that check your other programs. Write them once and
run them every time you change something, and you find out immediately if
you've broken anything. Python's `unittest` module is built in. Today: assert
statements, test classes, and how to read the results.

sections.heading: assert: the simplest test
sections.body:
`assert condition, message` does nothing if the condition is true and
raises AssertionError if it's false. A row of asserts at the bottom of a
file is a perfectly good first test suite.
sections.code:
def is_palindrome(s):
    s = s.lower()
    return s == s[::-1]

assert is_palindrome('racecar') == True
assert is_palindrome('hello') == False
assert is_palindrome('Level'), 'should ignore case'
print('All assertions passed')

sections.heading: A TestCase class
sections.body:
Subclass `unittest.TestCase`. Every method whose name starts with `test`
is a test. Use `self.assertTrue`, `self.assertFalse`, `self.assertEqual`
and friends; they give better messages than plain `assert`.

sections.heading: Reading the output
sections.body:
Each test prints one character: `.` for pass, `F` for a failed assertion,
`E` for an unexpected exception. Then a summary. The output goes to
stderr, so in this app it shows under the "also written to stderr"
heading. That's normal.

`unittest.main(argv=['x'], exit=False)` is used here instead of the usual
`unittest.main()` because this app runs your code with its own arguments
and `exit=False` stops it from ending the program early.

sections.heading: setUp: shared preparation
sections.body:
`setUp` runs before every test method. Anything you attach to `self`
there is available in each test. It keeps the tests short and stops you
repeating the same three lines.

sections.heading: assertRaises: testing that errors happen
sections.body:
Sometimes the right behaviour is to raise. `with self.assertRaises(X):`
passes only if the code inside raises that exception.

watch_out: Test methods must start with `test`. A method called `check_thing` is silently ignored.
`self.assertEqual(a, b)` gives a useful message showing both values. `assert a == b` just says it failed.
In this app, use `unittest.main(argv=['x'], exit=False)`. Plain `unittest.main()` reads the app's arguments and exits early.
Test output on stderr isn't an error. Look for OK or FAILED at the end.
